claim: The study investigated early vegetative growth of 249 natural Arabidopsis thaliana accessions in cold, nonfreezing temperatures.
source: We investigated early vegetative growth of natural Arabidopsis thaliana accessions in cold, nonfreezing temperatures, similar to temperatures these plants naturally encounter in fall at northern latitudes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the experimental design and number of accessions studied.

claim: Accessions from northern latitudes produced larger seedlings than accessions from southern latitudes.
source: We found that accessions from northern latitudes produced larger seedlings than accessions from southern latitudes, partly as a result of larger seed size.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Larger seedling size in northern accessions is partly due to larger seed size.
source: We found that accessions from northern latitudes produced larger seedlings than accessions from southern latitudes, partly as a result of larger seed size.
evidence: The abstract explicitly attributes part of the seedling size difference to seed size.

claim: Northern accessions showed slower subsequent vegetative growth when exposed to colder temperatures.
source: However, their subsequent vegetative growth when exposed to colder temperatures was slower.
evidence: The abstract presents this as an experimental observation.

claim: The growth difference between northern and southern accessions is too large to be explained by random population differentiation.
source: The difference was too large to be explained by random population differentiation, and is thus suggestive of local adaptation, a notion that is further supported by substantial transcriptome and metabolome changes in northern accessions.
evidence: The abstract presents this as an inference from statistical analysis.

claim: The growth differences suggest local adaptation.
source: The difference was too large to be explained by random population differentiation, and is thus suggestive of local adaptation, a notion that is further supported by substantial transcriptome and metabolome changes in northern accessions.
evidence: The abstract presents this as an inference from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Northern accessions show substantial transcriptome changes.
source: The difference was too large to be explained by random population differentiation, and is thus suggestive of local adaptation, a notion that is further supported by substantial transcriptome and metabolome changes in northern accessions.
evidence: The abstract states this as an experimental finding.

claim: Northern accessions show substantial metabolome changes.
source: The difference was too large to be explained by random population differentiation, and is thus suggestive of local adaptation, a notion that is further supported by substantial transcriptome and metabolome changes in northern accessions.
evidence: The abstract states this as an experimental finding.

claim: The reduced growth of northern accessions is an adaptive response.
source: We hypothesize that the reduced growth of northern accessions is an adaptive response and a consequence of reallocating resources toward cold acclimation and winter survival.
evidence: The abstract explicitly presents this as a hypothesis.

claim: Reduced growth in northern accessions is a consequence of reallocating resources toward cold acclimation and winter survival.
source: We hypothesize that the reduced growth of northern accessions is an adaptive response and a consequence of reallocating resources toward cold acclimation and winter survival.
evidence: The abstract explicitly presents this as a hypothesis.

claim: Life history strategies in plants have evolved to maximize fitness but are constrained by trade-offs between growth, survival, and reproduction.
source: These strategies have evolved to maximize fitness, but are constrained by trade-offs between components such as growth, survival, and reproduction (Lande, 1982; Stearns, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Life history variation in Arabidopsis thaliana has been linked to climate parameters.
source: While most life history studies investigate differences between species, there is also variation found within species, including in Arabidopsis thaliana, where life history variation has been linked to climate parameters (Estarague et al., 2022; Vasseur et al., 2018; Sartori et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Seed dormancy and flowering time play important roles in local adaptation in A. thaliana.
source: Local adaptation studies in A. thaliana have found important roles for life history traits such as seed dormancy and flowering time (Takou et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Temperature is a major regulator of seed dormancy and flowering time.
source: Temperature is a major regulator of these traits and local populations are adapted to their local climate (Martínez-Berdeja et al., 2020; Simpson and Dean, 2002; Hepworth et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Local populations are adapted to their local climate.
source: Temperature is a major regulator of these traits and local populations are adapted to their local climate (Martínez-Berdeja et al., 2020; Simpson and Dean, 2002; Hepworth et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Plant growth is affected by temperature.
source: Plant growth is also affected by temperature, and previous studies have detected genetic variation underlying growth-related traits (Bac-Molenaar et al., 2015; Marchadier et al., 2019), as well as signals of polygenic adaptation (Wieters et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous studies have detected genetic variation underlying growth-related traits.
source: Plant growth is also affected by temperature, and previous studies have detected genetic variation underlying growth-related traits (Bac-Molenaar et al., 2015; Marchadier et al., 2019), as well as signals of polygenic adaptation (Wieters et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous studies have detected signals of polygenic adaptation in growth-related traits.
source: Plant growth is also affected by temperature, and previous studies have detected genetic variation underlying growth-related traits (Bac-Molenaar et al., 2015; Marchadier et al., 2019), as well as signals of polygenic adaptation (Wieters et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Growth can be seen as the end sum of a vast number of physiological processes.
source: Growth can be seen as the end sum of a vast number of physiological processes.
evidence: This is a general statement about the nature of growth based on biological knowledge.

claim: Physiological processes underlying growth are genetically determined but can be heavily influenced by environmental conditions.
source: All of these are genetically determined but can also be heavily influenced by environmental conditions (Bac-Molenaar et al., 2015; Fritz et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Growth is genetically a complex trait and enormously plastic.
source: Growth is therefore not only genetically a complex trait but also enormously plastic.
evidence: This is an inference from the previous statements about genetic and environmental influences.

claim: Passive plasticity occurs when conditions are so adverse that growth reaches a physiological limit.
source: The most straightforward environmental effect is when conditions are so adverse that growth reaches a physiological limit, making it impossible for the plant to grow any further. This is called 'passive plasticity' (Forsman, 2015; van Kleunen and Fischer, 2005).
evidence: This definition is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Active plasticity occurs when plants actively inhibit growth upon deteriorating environmental conditions.
source: Yet, when survival is at stake, it may also be in the interest of the plant to actively inhibit growth upon deteriorating environmental conditions (Claeys and Inzé, 2013), called 'active plasticity' (Forsman, 2015; van Kleunen and Fischer, 2005).
evidence: This definition is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Vegetative growth ultimately determines photosynthetic surface and thus energy input that can be invested in the next generation.
source: Since vegetative growth ultimately determines photosynthetic surface and thus energy input that can be invested in the next generation, it is directly related to fitness, and is typically in trade-off with survival.
evidence: This is a statement based on general biological knowledge.

claim: Vegetative growth is directly related to fitness and is typically in trade-off with survival.
source: Since vegetative growth ultimately determines photosynthetic surface and thus energy input that can be invested in the next generation, it is directly related to fitness, and is typically in trade-off with survival.
evidence: This is a statement based on general biological knowledge.

claim: Cold acclimation is a mechanism in which decreasing temperatures induce freezing tolerance in preparation for winter.
source: Cold acclimation is a well-studied mechanism in plants, in which decreasing temperatures induce freezing tolerance in preparation for winter (Thomashow, 1999; Hughes and Dunn, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cold acclimation temperature response is typically studied at 4°C but has been observed in temperatures up to 12°C.
source: This temperature response is typically studied at 4°C, but has been observed in temperatures up to 12°C (Bond et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Increased freezing tolerance is accomplished by changing membrane composition.
source: The increased freezing tolerance is accomplished by changing membrane composition, producing cryoprotective polypeptides such as COR15A (Artus et al., 1996; Steponkus et al., 1998) and accumulating compatible solutes with cryoprotective properties such as raffinose, sucrose, and proline (Nanjo et al., 1999; Gilmour et al., 2000; Taji et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased freezing tolerance is accomplished by producing cryoprotective polypeptides such as COR15A.
source: The increased freezing tolerance is accomplished by changing membrane composition, producing cryoprotective polypeptides such as COR15A (Artus et al., 1996; Steponkus et al., 1998) and accumulating compatible solutes with cryoprotective properties such as raffinose, sucrose, and proline (Nanjo et al., 1999; Gilmour et al., 2000; Taji et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased freezing tolerance is accomplished by accumulating compatible solutes with cryoprotective properties such as raffinose, sucrose, and proline.
source: The increased freezing tolerance is accomplished by changing membrane composition, producing cryoprotective polypeptides such as COR15A (Artus et al., 1996; Steponkus et al., 1998) and accumulating compatible solutes with cryoprotective properties such as raffinose, sucrose, and proline (Nanjo et al., 1999; Gilmour et al., 2000; Taji et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CBF1/DREB1b, CBF2/DREB1c, and CBF3/DREB1a are main regulators of cold acclimation.
source: Main regulators of cold acclimation are CBF1/DREB1b, CBF2/DREB1c, and CBF3/DREB1a, three AP2/ERF transcription factors, for which allelic variation in CBF2 has been linked to natural variation in freezing tolerance (Oakley et al., 2014; Park et al., 2018; Alonso-Blanco et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Allelic variation in CBF2 has been linked to natural variation in freezing tolerance.
source: Main regulators of cold acclimation are CBF1/DREB1b, CBF2/DREB1c, and CBF3/DREB1a, three AP2/ERF transcription factors, for which allelic variation in CBF2 has been linked to natural variation in freezing tolerance (Oakley et al., 2014; Park et al., 2018; Alonso-Blanco et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The experiment compared vegetative growth of 249 accessions grown in daily maximum temperatures of 16 and 6°C for 3 weeks following seedling establishment.
source: Here, we investigated the role of growth in adaptation to cold temperatures by comparing vegetative growth of 249 accessions (Figure 1) grown in daily maximum temperatures of 16 and 6°C for a period of 3 weeks following seedling establishment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Rosette growth of each plant was measured twice a day during temperature treatments using automated phenotyping.
source: Rosette growth of each plant was measured twice a day during temperature treatments using automated phenotyping.
evidence: This describes the measurement methodology.

claim: The experiment generated rosette growth estimates at high temporal resolution in two ecologically realistic temperature conditions.
source: The experiment generated rosette growth estimates at a high temporal resolution in two ecologically realistic temperature conditions in a wide set of accessions, allowing us to look for patterns of local adaptation.
evidence: This describes the nature of the data generated.

claim: The experiment yielded dense time-series growth data for over 7000 individual plants.
source: Our highly replicated experiment yielded dense (two measurements per day) time-series growth data for over 7000 individual plants (5 replicate plants × 249 accessions × 2 treatments × 3 replicate experiments).
evidence: This describes the scale of the experimental data.

claim: A power-law function describes early stages of plant growth especially well.
source: Growth according to a power-law function typically describes early stages of plant growth especially well (Paine et al., 2012), and our rosette size measurements were no exception (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and confirmed by the authors' data.

claim: All accessions grew faster when it was warmer.
source: As expected, all accessions grew faster when it was warmer.
evidence: This is presented as an experimental observation.

claim: Broad-sense heritability is 0.41 for initial size.
source: The observed phenotypic variation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) is to a large extent explained by genetic variation; broad-sense heritabilities are 0.41 for initial size, and 0.57 and 0.32 for growth rate at 16 and 6°C, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated value from the experimental data.

claim: Broad-sense heritability is 0.57 for growth rate at 16°C.
source: The observed phenotypic variation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) is to a large extent explained by genetic variation; broad-sense heritabilities are 0.41 for initial size, and 0.57 and 0.32 for growth rate at 16 and 6°C, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated value from the experimental data.

claim: Broad-sense heritability is 0.32 for growth rate at 6°C.
source: The observed phenotypic variation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) is to a large extent explained by genetic variation; broad-sense heritabilities are 0.41 for initial size, and 0.57 and 0.32 for growth rate at 16 and 6°C, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated value from the experimental data.

claim: Climate variables showing the strongest correlations with growth parameters were linked to winter temperatures.
source: The climate variables showing the strongest correlations with the different growth parameters were linked to winter temperatures (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), also when correlations were corrected for population structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis shown in figures.

claim: Mean temperature during the coldest quarter was most strongly correlated with growth parameter estimates.
source: In particular, the mean temperature during the coldest quarter (henceforth referred to as 'winter temperature') was most strongly correlated with our parameter estimates, and we focus on it in what follows.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Winter temperature explained 32.7% of the variation in initial size in a random-effect model.
source: In a random-effect model, winter temperature explained 32.7% of the variation in initial size, whereas seed size explained 11.9%.
evidence: This is a statistical result from modeling analysis.

claim: Seed size explained 11.9% of the variation in initial size in a random-effect model.
source: In a random-effect model, winter temperature explained 32.7% of the variation in initial size, whereas seed size explained 11.9%.
evidence: This is a statistical result from modeling analysis.

claim: Seed size alone cannot explain the geographic pattern observed for M0.
source: The precise role of seed size in initial growth is surely a topic that would benefit from further studies, but for the purpose of this study, it is clear that seed size alone cannot explain the geographic pattern we observe for M0 and that there must be a role for variation in growth rate during the very initial phases of seedling growth.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analyses showing seed size explains only part of the variation.

claim: The higher growth rates of accessions from warmer climates prove that resources are not limiting.
source: The higher growth rates of accessions from warmer climates prove that resources are not limiting, suggesting that the northern lines are actively inhibiting their growth, and that growing slower may be beneficial in colder climates, perhaps in preparation for winter.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that southern accessions can grow faster.

claim: Northern lines are actively inhibiting their growth.
source: The higher growth rates of accessions from warmer climates prove that resources are not limiting, suggesting that the northern lines are actively inhibiting their growth, and that growing slower may be beneficial in colder climates, perhaps in preparation for winter.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that resources are not limiting.

claim: Growing slower may be beneficial in colder climates, perhaps in preparation for winter.
source: The higher growth rates of accessions from warmer climates prove that resources are not limiting, suggesting that the northern lines are actively inhibiting their growth, and that growing slower may be beneficial in colder climates, perhaps in preparation for winter.
evidence: This is speculation about the adaptive benefit of slower growth.

claim: Metabolite measurements showed clear differences between accessions from cold and warm regions.
source: Just like the observed geographic pattern of the growth rates, metabolite measurements taken at the final day of our experiment and presented in an earlier publication (Weiszmann et al., 2020) showed clear differences between accessions from cold and warm regions, and many of these differences involved metabolites with a known role in cold acclimation.
evidence: This refers to data from a previous publication by the same group.

claim: Many metabolite differences between cold and warm region accessions involved metabolites with a known role in cold acclimation.
source: Just like the observed geographic pattern of the growth rates, metabolite measurements taken at the final day of our experiment and presented in an earlier publication (Weiszmann et al., 2020) showed clear differences between accessions from cold and warm regions, and many of these differences involved metabolites with a known role in cold acclimation.
evidence: This refers to data from a previous publication by the same group.

claim: Expression of different subsets of cold-acclimation genes shows clear correlations with winter temperature of origin.
source: Expression of different subsets of the selected cold-acclimation genes shows clear correlations with winter temperature of origin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the transcriptome analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Genes that were previously found to be upregulated upon cold exposure showed higher expression in accessions from cold climates.
source: In particular, the genes that were previously found to be upregulated upon cold exposure showed higher expression in accessions from cold climates (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the transcriptome analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Accessions from cold climates likely differ in their ability to cope with freezing temperatures upon cold treatment.
source: Since the expression of these cold-acclimation genes has been linked to the strength of cold acclimation in previous experiments (Park et al., 2015; Vogel et al., 2005), these accessions likely differ in their ability to cope with freezing temperatures upon cold treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression data and previous literature.

claim: Geographic differentiation exists in the expression of known cold-response genes.
source: More generally, it establishes that geographic differentiation exists in the expression of known cold-response genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the transcriptome analysis.

claim: Accessions from warm climates may activate cold acclimation as a stress response rather than as a preventive measure.
source: Accessions from warm climates may instead activate cold acclimation as a stress response rather than as a preventive measure.
evidence: This is speculation based on the gene expression patterns observed.

claim: Metabolites involved in cold acclimation such as raffinose, sucrose, and proline were found in higher concentrations in accessions from colder climates.
source: Metabolites involved in cold acclimation such as raffinose, sucrose, and proline were found in higher concentrations in accessions from colder climates (Weiszmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This refers to data from a previous publication by the same group.

claim: Accessions from colder environments are relocating more energy and resources from growth towards preparations for upcoming freezing temperatures.
source: We believe that accessions from colder environments are relocating more energy and resources from growth towards preparations for upcoming freezing temperatures, which is a clear example of active plasticity (Forsman, 2015; van Kleunen and Fischer, 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by citations to the concept of active plasticity.

claim: Resource reallocation from growth to cold acclimation preparation is a clear example of active plasticity.
source: We believe that accessions from colder environments are relocating more energy and resources from growth towards preparations for upcoming freezing temperatures, which is a clear example of active plasticity (Forsman, 2015; van Kleunen and Fischer, 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to the concept of active plasticity.

claim: Resource reallocation results in stronger cold acclimation and consequently increased freezing tolerance in accessions from colder regions.
source: Even though we have no direct survival measurements, we speculate that this results in stronger cold acclimation and consequently increased freezing tolerance in the accessions from colder regions.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: Accessions originating from colder environments show increased freezing tolerance upon cold acclimation.
source: Indeed, accessions originating from colder environments show increased freezing tolerance upon cold acclimation (Zhen et al., 2011; Zuther et al., 2012; Hannah et al., 2006; Horton et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Northern and colder regions favor slower growing, more stress-tolerant plants.
source: This fits with observations of northern and colder regions favoring slower growing, more stress-tolerant plants (Vasseur et al., 2018; Estarague et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Winter temperatures are a major determinant of suitable habitats for A. thaliana.
source: Also, biogeographic studies in A. thaliana found that winter temperatures are a major determinant of suitable habitats for this species (Hoffmann, 2002; Yim et al., 2022), and reciprocal transplant experiments detected an important role for freezing tolerance in fitness variation in northern sites (Ågren and Schemske, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Reciprocal transplant experiments detected an important role for freezing tolerance in fitness variation in northern sites.
source: Also, biogeographic studies in A. thaliana found that winter temperatures are a major determinant of suitable habitats for this species (Hoffmann, 2002; Yim et al., 2022), and reciprocal transplant experiments detected an important role for freezing tolerance in fitness variation in northern sites (Ågren and Schemske, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The reduced growth plasticity observed for accessions from colder climates is due to the stronger growth reduction at 16°C in these accessions compared to accessions from warmer climates.
source: We speculate that the reduced growth plasticity observed for accessions from colder climates is due to the stronger growth reduction at 16°C in these accessions compared to accessions from warmer climates.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: Accessions from colder climates may be anticipating winter at 16°C, whereas accessions from warmer climates do not.
source: They may well be anticipating winter, whereas accessions from warmer climates do not, and hence show a stronger difference between 16 and 6°C.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed patterns.

claim: It is impossible to rule out that accessions from colder climates grow slower due to reduced resource efficiency as they become larger.
source: Although both metabolite and gene expression data suggest an involvement of cold acclimation, we note that it is impossible to rule out that accessions from colder climates grow slower due to reduced resource efficiency as they become larger or, for example, increase leaf thickness (Adams et al., 2016).
evidence: This acknowledges an alternative explanation that cannot be ruled out.

claim: Genetic variation in the CBF2 gene is one of the drivers for adaptation to freezing stress.
source: There is strong evidence from QTL mapping that genetic variation in the CBF2 gene is one of the drivers for adaptation to freezing stress (Oakley et al., 2014; Gehan et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: No associations with the CBF loci were detected in the GWAS analysis for growth phenotypes.
source: Here, we looked at growth phenotypes and did not detect associations with the CBF loci.
evidence: This is a result from the GWAS analysis.

claim: The transcriptome analysis picked up a role for CBF and other known cold-acclimation genes.
source: In the transcriptome analysis, we did pick up a role for CBF and other known cold-acclimation genes.
evidence: This is a result from the transcriptome analysis.

claim: The most significant locus detected in the GWAS analysis for growth rate at 16°C lies in the vicinity of COL5.
source: The most significant locus detected in our GWAS analysis (for growth rate at 16°C) lies in the vicinity of COL5, a gene that is part of a leaf growth regulatory network (Vercruyssen et al., 2014) and whose expression is induced by both cold treatment and CBF1, CBF2, and CBF3 overexpression (Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a result from the GWAS analysis with supporting citations.

claim: COL5 is part of a leaf growth regulatory network.
source: The most significant locus detected in our GWAS analysis (for growth rate at 16°C) lies in the vicinity of COL5, a gene that is part of a leaf growth regulatory network (Vercruyssen et al., 2014) and whose expression is induced by both cold treatment and CBF1, CBF2, and CBF3 overexpression (Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: COL5 expression is induced by both cold treatment and CBF1, CBF2, and CBF3 overexpression.
source: The most significant locus detected in our GWAS analysis (for growth rate at 16°C) lies in the vicinity of COL5, a gene that is part of a leaf growth regulatory network (Vercruyssen et al., 2014) and whose expression is induced by both cold treatment and CBF1, CBF2, and CBF3 overexpression (Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Adaptive differentiation was detected for initial size, growth rate at 16°C, and its temperature response.
source: Adaptive differentiation was detected for initial size and for growth rate at 16°C and its temperature response.
evidence: This is a result from the adaptive differentiation analysis.

claim: The adaptive differentiation for initial size along PC6 stems from higher initial sizes in Swedish accessions compared to central European accessions.
source: The adaptive differentiation for initial size along PC6 seems to stem from higher initial sizes in Swedish accessions compared to central European accessions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the adaptive differentiation results.

claim: The adaptive differentiation along PC5 is driven by lower growth rate temperature responses in Asian and northern Swedish accessions in contrast to higher growth rates in a subset of southern Swedish accessions.
source: The adaptive differentiation along PC5 seems to be driven by the lower growth rate temperature responses in Asian and northern Swedish accessions in contrast to higher growth rates in a subset of southern Swedish accessions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the adaptive differentiation results.

claim: Accessions from northern Sweden and Asia come from the coldest climates in the study set.
source: The accessions in our set that come from northern Sweden and Asia hail from the coldest climates.
evidence: This is a description of the accessions based on their geographic origin.

claim: The slower growth measured in accessions from colder climates reflects relocation of resources from growth towards cold acclimation.
source: We speculated that the slower growth measured in accessions from colder climates reflects relocation of resources from growth towards cold acclimation.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation in the Discussion.

claim: Metabolome and gene expression data are consistent with accessions from colder climates preparing for a harsh winter.
source: Both metabolome and gene expression data are consistent with accessions from colder climates preparing for a harsh winter.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the metabolome and transcriptome data.

claim: The growth of northern lines is affected less than southern lines by switching from 16°C to 6°C.
source: In our temperature experiment, we see that the growth of northern lines is affected less than southern lines by switching from 16°C to 6°C.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The conclusion that slower growth is likely adaptive in populations facing fiercer winters is in line with recent results of Wieters et al., 2021.
source: Our conclusion that slower growth is likely adaptive in populations facing fiercer winters is in line with recent results of Wieters et al., 2021, who concluded that the reduced growth in northern lines was adaptive and not a consequence of an accumulation of deleterious mutations at the species border.
evidence: This statement compares the current findings with previous research.

claim: Wieters et al., 2021 concluded that reduced growth in northern lines was adaptive and not a consequence of an accumulation of deleterious mutations at the species border.
source: Our conclusion that slower growth is likely adaptive in populations facing fiercer winters is in line with recent results of Wieters et al., 2021, who concluded that the reduced growth in northern lines was adaptive and not a consequence of an accumulation of deleterious mutations at the species border.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited paper.

claim: If slower growth were a consequence of accumulated deleterious mutations, we would expect to see slower growth also during the initial seedling establishment.
source: If slower growth were indeed a consequence of accumulated deleterious mutations, we would expect to see slower growth also during the initial seedling establishment, which we measured here as the initial size.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected under an alternative hypothesis.

claim: Fast seedling establishment is a potential adaptation for short growth seasons, which often coincide with colder climates.
source: We speculate that the fast seedling establishment is a potential adaptation for short growth seasons, which often coincide with colder climates (high latitude or high altitude).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: Larger seeds may provide more nutrients to initiate faster seedling establishment.
source: This fast seedling establishment seems to be partly supported by larger seeds. These larger seeds may provide more nutrients to initiate faster seedling establishment, while this is of less importance in warmer climates with longer growth seasons.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism linking seed size to seedling establishment.

claim: The adaptation of growth to local climates is likely to be influenced by a trade-off with cold acclimation.
source: The adaptation of growth to local climates is likely to be influenced by a trade-off with cold acclimation.
evidence: This is an inference from the data and discussion.

claim: General growth-survival trade-offs have long been observed and are described in general ecological strategy schemes such as Grime's C-S-R triangle.
source: General growth-survival trade-offs have long been observed and are described in general ecological strategy schemes such as Grime's C-S-R triangle (Grime, 1979) and the leaf–height–seed scheme (Westoby, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established ecological theory.

claim: Specific trade-offs between growth and cold/frost survival were observed for wheat.
source: Specific trade-offs between growth and cold/frost survival were observed for wheat (Hayes and Aamodt, 1927; Quisenberry, 1931), alfalfa (Castonguay et al., 2006), Dactylis glomerata (Bristiel et al., 2018), and multiple tree species (Koehler et al., 2012; Loehle, 1998; Molina-Montenegro et al., 2012; Savage and Cavender-Bares, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Specific trade-offs between growth and cold/frost survival were observed for alfalfa.
source: Specific trade-offs between growth and cold/frost survival were observed for wheat (Hayes and Aamodt, 1927; Quisenberry, 1931), alfalfa (Castonguay et al., 2006), Dactylis glomerata (Bristiel et al., 2018), and multiple tree species (Koehler et al., 2012; Loehle, 1998; Molina-Montenegro et al., 2012; Savage and Cavender-Bares, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Specific trade-offs between growth and cold/frost survival were observed for Dactylis glomerata.
source: Specific trade-offs between growth and cold/frost survival were observed for wheat (Hayes and Aamodt, 1927; Quisenberry, 1931), alfalfa (Castonguay et al., 2006), Dactylis glomerata (Bristiel et al., 2018), and multiple tree species (Koehler et al., 2012; Loehle, 1998; Molina-Montenegro et al., 2012; Savage and Cavender-Bares, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Specific trade-offs between growth and cold/frost survival were observed for multiple tree species.
source: Specific trade-offs between growth and cold/frost survival were observed for wheat (Hayes and Aamodt, 1927; Quisenberry, 1931), alfalfa (Castonguay et al., 2006), Dactylis glomerata (Bristiel et al., 2018), and multiple tree species (Koehler et al., 2012; Loehle, 1998; Molina-Montenegro et al., 2012; Savage and Cavender-Bares, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Higher expression of genes involved in cold acclimation was observed in accessions from colder regions.
source: Here, we observed higher expression of genes involved in cold acclimation in accessions from colder regions.
evidence: This is a result from the transcriptome analysis.

claim: Higher expression of cold-acclimation genes is clearest at 6°C but is also happening at 16°C.
source: This is clearest at 6°C, but is also happening at 16°C, suggesting that activation of cold acclimation is stronger in accessions from cold climates and may be triggered more easily.
evidence: This is an observation from the transcriptome data.

claim: Activation of cold acclimation is stronger in accessions from cold climates and may be triggered more easily.
source: This is clearest at 6°C, but is also happening at 16°C, suggesting that activation of cold acclimation is stronger in accessions from cold climates and may be triggered more easily.
evidence: This is an inference from the transcriptome data.

claim: Seeds of 249 natural accessions were sown on sieved substrate.
source: Seeds of 249 natural accessions (Figure 1—source data 1) of A. thaliana described in the 1001 genomes project (1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016) were sown on sieved (6 mm) substrate (Einheitserde ED63).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Pots were filled with 71.5 g ± 1.5 g of soil to ensure homogenous packing.
source: Pots were filled with 71.5 g ± 1.5 g of soil to ensure homogenous packing.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Temperature treatments were started by transferring seedlings to either 6 or 16°C.
source: The temperature treatments were started by transferring the seedlings to either 6 or 16°C.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Temperatures fluctuated diurnally between 16–21°C, 0.5–6°C, and 8–16°C for the 21°C initial growth conditions and the 6 and 16°C treatments, respectively.
source: To simulate natural conditions, temperatures fluctuated diurnally between 16–21°C, 0.5–6°C, and 8–16°C for the 21°C initial growth conditions and the 6 and 16°C treatments, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology shown in a figure.

claim: Daylength was 9 hr during the 16 and 6°C treatments.
source: Daylength was 9 hr during the 16 and 6°C treatments.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Each temperature treatment was repeated in three independent experiments.
source: Each temperature treatment was repeated in three independent experiments.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Five replicate plants were grown for every genotype per experiment.
source: Five replicate plants were grown for every genotype per experiment.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Plants were randomly distributed across the growth chamber with an independent randomization pattern for each experiment.
source: Plants were randomly distributed across the growth chamber with an independent randomization pattern for each experiment.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Plants were photographed twice a day (1 hr after/before lights switched on/off) during the temperature treatments using an RGB camera.
source: During the temperature treatments (14–35 days after stratification), plants were photographed twice a day (1 hr after/before lights switched on/off), using an RGB camera (IDS uEye UI-548xRE-C; 5MP) mounted to a robotic arm.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Rosette areas were extracted from plant images using Lemnatec OS software.
source: Rosette areas were extracted from the plant images using Lemnatec OS (LemnaTec GmbH, Aachen, Germany) software.
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology.

claim: Datapoints with smaller rosette areas than earlier time points (negative growth) were discarded from further analyses.
source: Plant growth profiles were visually inspected, and datapoints with smaller rosette areas than earlier time points (negative growth) were discarded from further analyses.
evidence: This describes the data quality control procedure.

claim: Whole rosettes were harvested at 35 days after stratification, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at –80°C.
source: At 35 days after stratification, whole rosettes were harvested, immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at –80°C until further analysis.
evidence: This describes the sample collection methodology.

claim: The power-law model was chosen over the exponential model based on Akaike information criterion and likelihood ratio test.
source: Based on Akaike information criterion and likelihood ratio test generated by the anova function (Table 1), we decided to use the power-law model for further analyses.
evidence: This describes the model selection procedure with reference to a table.

claim: The power-law model had a likelihood ratio statistic of 202.061 and p-value <0.001 compared to the exponential model.
source: Based on Akaike information criterion and likelihood ratio test generated by the anova function (Table 1), we decided to use the power-law model for further analyses.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: Accession was added as fixed effect for initial size and growth rate in the model.
source: Accession was added as fixed effect for initial size and growth rate, temperature and accession × temperature interactions were added as fixed effects for growth rate only.
evidence: This describes the statistical model structure.

claim: Temperature and accession × temperature interactions were added as fixed effects for growth rate only.
source: Accession was added as fixed effect for initial size and growth rate, temperature and accession × temperature interactions were added as fixed effects for growth rate only.
evidence: This describes the statistical model structure.

claim: The temperature response of the growth rate was calculated for each accession as the slope between the growth rate at 16 and 6°C.
source: The 'temperature response' of the growth rate was calculated for each accession as the slope between the growth rate at 16 and 6°C.
evidence: This describes the calculation methodology.

claim: Climate data were downloaded from https://www.worldclim.org.
source: The different phenotypes were correlated with each of the different (bio)climate variables downloaded from https://www.worldclim.org (Fick and Hijmans, 2017).
evidence: This describes the data source for climate variables.

claim: Correlations were calculated as Pearson's correlations using the cor function in R.
source: Correlations were calculated as Pearson's correlations using the cor function in R (4.0.3; R Development Core Team, 2017).
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology.

claim: Population structure-corrected correlations used a mixed-effects model with the kinship matrix as random effect.
source: For the population–structure-corrected correlations, we used a mixed-effects model as implemented in the lmekin function from the coxme (2.2.16; Therneau, 2020) package with phenotype as dependent variable, climate variable as fixed effects, and the kinship matrix as random effect.
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology for correcting for population structure.

claim: The kinship matrix was based on SNPs from the 1001 genomes consortium and was calculated using 'mixmogam'.
source: The kinship matrix was based on the SNPs from the 1001 genomes consortium (1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016) and was calculated using 'mixmogam' (https://github.com/bvilhjal/mixmogam; Vilhjalmsson, 2019) based on Kang et al., 2010.
evidence: This describes the methodology for calculating the kinship matrix.

claim: Seed size measurements were limited to 123 Swedish accessions that overlapped with the growth dataset.
source: We used the seeds produced by Kerdaffrec et al., 2016 and limited our measurements to the set of 123 Swedish accessions that overlapped with our growth dataset.
evidence: This describes the seed size measurement methodology.

claim: Mother plants for seed production were grown for 8 weeks at 4°C under long-day conditions to ensure proper vernalization.
source: After seed stratification for four days at 4°C in darkness, mother plants were grown for 8 weeks at 4°C under long-day conditions (16 hr light; 8 hr dark) to ensure proper vernalization.
evidence: This describes the seed production methodology.

claim: Temperature was raised to 21°C (light) and 16°C (dark) for flowering and seed ripening.
source: Temperature was raised to 21°C (light) and 16°C (dark) for flowering and seed ripening.
evidence: This describes the seed production methodology.

claim: Seeds were kept in darkness at 16°C and 30% relative humidity from harvest until seed size measurements.
source: Seeds were kept in darkness at 16°C and 30% relative humidity, from the harvest until seed size measurements.
evidence: This describes the seed storage conditions.

claim: About 200–300 seeds were sprinkled on 12 × 12 cm² transparent Petri dishes for each genotype.
source: For each genotype, three replicates were pooled and about 200–300 seeds were sprinkled on 12 × 12 cm2, transparent Petri dishes.
evidence: This describes the seed size measurement methodology.

claim: Image acquisition was performed by scanning dishes on a cluster of eight Epson V600 scanners.
source: Image acquisition was performed as described in Exposito-Alonso et al., 2018 by scanning dishes on a cluster of eight Epson V600 scanners.
evidence: This describes the seed size measurement methodology with a citation.

claim: The resulting 1200 dpi .tiff images were analyzed with ImageJ software.
source: The resulting 1200 dpi .tiff images were analyzed with the ImageJ software (2.1.0/1.53c).
evidence: This describes the image analysis methodology.

claim: Random samples from each replicate experiment for both temperatures were taken for eight accessions to profile the transcriptome with RNA-sequencing.
source: 35 days after stratification, rosette tissue of all plants were harvested and flash frozen in liquid nitrogen. Random samples from each replicate experiment for both temperatures were taken for eight accessions to profile the transcriptome with RNA-sequencing.
evidence: This describes the transcriptome profiling methodology.

claim: Total RNA was extracted using the KingFisher Duo Prime System together with a high-performance RNA bead isolation kit.
source: Total RNA was extracted using the KingFisher Duo Prime System (Thermo Fisher Scientific) together with a high-performance RNA bead isolation kit (Molecular Biology Service, VBC Core Facilities, Vienna).
evidence: This describes the RNA extraction methodology.

claim: RNA quantity was determined using Fluorometer Qubit 4 and Qubit RNA BR Kit.
source: To determine the quantity of RNA, we used Fluorometer Qubit 4 (Invitrogen) and Qubit RNA BR Kit (Invitrogen).
evidence: This describes the RNA quantification methodology.

claim: For each sample, 1 µg of total RNA was treated with the poly(A) RNA Selection Kit and eluted in 12 µl of Nuclease-Free Water.
source: For each sample, 1 µg of total RNA was treated with the poly(A) RNA Selection Kit (Lexogen) and eluted in 12 µl of Nuclease-Free Water.
evidence: This describes the RNA library preparation methodology.

claim: Libraries were prepared according to the NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit protocol and individually indexed with NEBNext Multiplex Oligos for Illumina.
source: Libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer's protocol in NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit (New England Biolabs) and individually indexed with NEBNext Multiplex Oligos for Illumina (New England Biolabs).
evidence: This describes the RNA library preparation methodology.

claim: Libraries were sequenced with an Illumina HiSeq2500 in paired-end mode with read length of 125 bp.
source: Libraries were sequenced with an Illumina HiSeq2500 in paired-end mode with read length of 125 bp.
evidence: This describes the RNA sequencing methodology.

claim: Gene expression was quantified using quasi-mapping in salmon (1.2.1).
source: Gene expression was quantified by using quasi-mapping in salmon (1.2.1; Patro et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the gene expression quantification methodology with a citation.

claim: Salmon indices were built separately for each accession incorporating SNP variation from the 1001 Genomes Consortium into the reference transcriptome.
source: The salmon indices were built separately for each accession as we incorporated the SNP variation from the 1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016 into the reference transcriptome.
evidence: This describes the gene expression quantification methodology.

claim: The heatmap was built using pheatmap (1.0.12) in R.
source: The heatmap was built using pheatmap (1.0.12; Kolde, 2019) in R (4.0.3; R Development Core Team, 2017).
evidence: This describes the data visualization methodology.

claim: Clustering was done by complete clustering on Euclidean distances for both rows and columns.
source: The clustering was done by complete clustering on Euclidean distances for both rows and columns.
evidence: This describes the clustering methodology.

claim: Gene clusters were defined by cutting the dendrogram in seven groups.
source: The gene clusters were defined by cutting the dendrogram in seven groups.
evidence: This describes the cluster definition methodology.

claim: Differential expression analysis was conducted with the DESeq2 package (1.30.0) in R.
source: Differential expression analysis was conducted with the DESeq2 package (1.30.0; Love et al., 2014) in R (4.0.3; R Development Core Team, 2017).
evidence: This describes the differential expression analysis methodology with a citation.

claim: Genes were considered differentially expressed when the adjusted p-value was <0.05.
source: Genes were considered differentially expressed when the adjusted p-value was <0.05.
evidence: This describes the threshold for differential expression.

claim: Metabolome profiling was conducted on all 249 accessions with samples taken 35 days after stratification.
source: Besides transcriptome profiling of eight accessions, we also conducted metabolome profiling on all 249 accessions. Samples for metabolome measurements were taken from the same experiments described in this study and, just like the transcriptome samples, were taken 35 days after stratification.
evidence: This describes the metabolome profiling methodology.

claim: Metabolome profiling results and detailed methodology are described in Weiszmann et al., 2020.
source: Results and detailed methodology are described in Weiszmann et al., 2020.
evidence: This refers to a previous publication for detailed methods.

claim: Variance explained by experiment was removed by including experiment as a fixed effect in the heritability model.
source: Because our accession estimates were corrected for experiment effects, we removed the variance explained by experiment by including experiment as a fixed effect.
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology for heritability calculation.

claim: Genome-wide association mapping was done using a mixed model with phenotype as dependent variable, genotype as fixed effect, and genetic relatedness as random factor.
source: Genome-wide association mapping was done for each of the growth parameters in both temperatures and also the temperature response for the growth rate. We used a mixed model with phenotype as dependent variable, genotype as fixed effect, and genetic relatedness as random factor.
evidence: This describes the GWAS methodology.

claim: Nonimputed SNPs obtained from the 1001 Genomes Consortium were used as genotypes in GWAS.
source: Nonimputed SNPs obtained from the 1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016 were used as genotypes.
evidence: This describes the genotype data used in GWAS.

claim: GWAS was run in GEMMA (0.98.3) with kinship matrix calculated as the centered relatedness matrix.
source: This model was run in GEMMA (0.98.3; Zhou and Stephens, 2012), with kinship matrix calculated as the centered relatedness matrix, as implemented in GEMMA.
evidence: This describes the GWAS software and methodology with a citation.

claim: Adaptive differentiation was tested with the method described by Josephs et al., 2019 using the quaint package.
source: Adaptive differentiation was tested with the method described by Josephs et al., 2019 and the accompanying quaint package (0.0.0.9; https://github.com/emjosephs/quaint; Josephs, 2020) in R (4.0.3; R Development Core Team, 2017).
evidence: This describes the adaptive differentiation testing methodology with citations.

claim: The kinship matrix for adaptive differentiation testing was calculated using the make_k function in the quaint package.
source: The kinship matrix was calculated using the make_k function in the quaint package.
evidence: This describes the methodology for calculating the kinship matrix.

claim: Genetic PCs were calculated from the eigen decomposition of the kinship matrix.
source: Genetic PCs were then calculated from the eigen decomposition of the kinship matrix.
evidence: This describes the methodology for calculating genetic principal components.

claim: Adaptive differentiation of each phenotype along the first 10 PCs was tested with the calcQpc function in the quaint package.
source: Adaptive differentiation of each phenotype along the first 10 PCs was tested with the calcQpc function in the quaint package.
evidence: This describes the adaptive differentiation testing methodology.

claim: PCs 11–248 were used to build the expected phenotypic differentiation under neutrality.
source: PCs 11–248 were used to build the expected phenotypic differentiation under neutrality.
evidence: This describes the methodology for building the neutral expectation.

claim: Scripts for the analysis can be found at https://github.com/picla/growth_16C_6C/.
source: Scripts can be found at https://github.com/picla/growth_16C_6C/; Clauw, 2022.
evidence: This provides the location of analysis scripts.

claim: Scripts for seed size analysis can be found at https://github.com/vevel/seed_size.
source: Scripts for seedsize analysis can be found at https://github.com/vevel/seed_size; Kerdaffrec, 2022.
evidence: This provides the location of seed size analysis scripts.

claim: All RNA-sequencing data were uploaded to SRA under http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/807069.
source: All RNA-sequencing were uploaded to SRA under http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/807069.
evidence: This provides the location of the RNA-seq data.

claim: All generated phenotyping data are filed under 10.5281/zenodo.6076948.
source: All generated phenotyping data are filed under 10.5281/zenodo.6076948.
evidence: This provides the location of the phenotyping data.

claim: CIPK21 encodes a CBL-interacting protein kinase that is upregulated in cold conditions and is involved in the salt and osmotic stress response.
source: CIPK21 encodes a CBL-interacting protein kinase that is upregulated in cold conditions and is involved in the salt and osmotic stress response (Pandey et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: MYB36 is a key regulator of root endodermal differentiation.
source: MYB36 is a key regulator of root endodermal differentiation (Liberman et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.
